units.title: Unit of observation, prediction time and label horizon
outcomes: State the unit of observation, the population, and the prediction context for a new problem in one short paragraph.
Specify prediction time, feature cutoff, action time, label horizon, and label availability for an hourly bike-demand task.
Explain why hour.csv and day.csv define different prediction contexts even though they describe the same system.
units.why: Every later choice inherits the prediction context. A row is not a prediction; the contract that binds a row to a decision time is.

study.title: Bike Sharing data dictionary and files
study.locator: Variables Table and Additional Variable Information: instant, dteday, hr, casual, registered, cnt, including the note that hr is absent from day.csv; Dataset Files: hour.csv, day.csv, Readme.txt; Dataset Characteristics with the no-missing-values statement

focus: The unit of observation is the row the decision attaches to: one district in housing, one system-hour in hour.csv, one system-day in day.csv. The two bike files are different populations of prediction contexts, not two views of one table.
Prediction time fixes which fields may be used. Anything stamped after the cutoff, including the horizon outcome itself, is unavailable even when it sits in the same CSV row.

Freshness is part of the context. State how old a model or feature may be before quality loss forces action, using Rule 8: Play Search degrades in under a month without updates, while identifier-free Whats Hot models export infrequently.

Checklist items 1 to 12 plus Get-the-data item 11 are the contract skeleton: objective, usage, current workaround, framing, measure, alignment, minimum performance, assumptions, and one untouched test set.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the one-paragraph contract for hourly bike demand: unit (one system-hour), population (dated hours in hour.csv), prediction time (top of the hour, before that hour rentals are known), cutoff (fields timestamped at or before prediction time only), horizon (the coming hour cnt), and action (fleet rebalancing). State why day.csv needs a separate contract.
traps: Treating each CSV row as a prediction without naming the decision time. hour.csv and day.csv can describe the same period at different grains and need different horizons and actions.
Reading dteday as a ready timestamp. In hour.csv it is a date string plus a separate hr column; the prediction instant is their combination, and parsing it is part of the contract.

Quoting the landing page count as the file count. The page states 17389 instances while the downloadable hour.csv holds 17379 data rows by direct count; count the file you downloaded and record the date.

selfTest.q: In the Housing Corp task, what is the unit of observation?
selfTest.a: One Californian district, which is one row of the housing data. The model predicts one median house value per district.

selfTest.q: Why do hour.csv and day.csv need separate prediction contracts?
selfTest.a: Different units (hour versus day), different horizons (next-hour versus next-day cnt), and different availability: hr exists only in hour.csv, and an hourly rebalancing action cannot wait for the day aggregate.

selfTest.q: A bike feature table refreshes daily but predictions run hourly. What must the contract state?
selfTest.a: The feature cutoff and the freshness requirement: hourly predictions reuse the last daily value, with a stated maximum age and a staleness check in the style of Rule 8.

selfTest.q: Where does the label horizon sit relative to prediction time in the bike contract?
selfTest.a: After it: cnt over the coming hour is realized after prediction time. The same-hour casual and registered counts are label parts, not features.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a one-page prediction contract with unit, prediction time, cutoff, horizon, and an availability table for the Bike Sharing rebuild.
units.stopWhen: You can write the hourly bike contract from memory, including why day.csv is excluded and which columns are unavailable at prediction time.

units.title: Targets, losses, metrics, decision rules and problem framing
outcomes: Distinguish the scientific question, prediction target, estimand, action, outcome, loss, metric, and product decision on a worked example.
Choose regression, classification, or an unsupervised framing from the decision thresholds, and defend a proxy label with its failure modes.
State success metrics separately from evaluation metrics, and keep prediction language associative rather than causal.
units.why: The loss and the decision rule decide what the model learns to care about. A perfect score on the wrong target still ships the wrong behavior.

next.note: Evaluate the chosen metric under a split that respects the decision process.
Deepen error and confusion-matrix metrics after framing them here.

study.title: Objectives versus metrics
study.locator: Rule 2: First, design and implement metrics; Rule 12: Do not overthink which objective you choose to directly optimize; Rule 13: Choose a simple, observable and attributable metric for your first objective

study.title: Framing checklist and task types
study.locator: Frame the problem, items 4 to 7: supervised/unsupervised and online/offline framing, performance measure, alignment with the business objective, minimum performance

study.title: Supervised and unsupervised task vocabulary
study.locator: Exercise Solutions 4, 5, and 8: regression and classification as the two most common supervised tasks, clustering/visualization/dimensionality-reduction/association as unsupervised tasks, spam detection as supervised

focus: Success metrics differ from evaluation metrics. Success is product behavior (feature opened 50 percent more; 20 percent more time on site); evaluation is model arithmetic (accuracy, RMSE, AUC). A better model score that does not move success is not progress.

Fixed thresholds call for classification, moving thresholds for regression. Squared error treats predictions 28 and 32 as equally good for truth 30 (both err by 4, error squared 4), yet the 30-view cache cutoff sends them to different caches.

Proxy labels substitute for unmeasurable goals (shared OR liked for usefulness). Each candidate in the table carries a stated failure mode: like-prediction misses users who never click like, popularity is not personalized, click prediction maximizes clickbait, watch time favors long videos.

Prediction language stays associative: predicts, is associated with. Acting on a prediction can change the outcome, as the clickbait paragraph shows engagement dropping after click-optimized ranking, so causal verbs need an experiment, not a model score.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, redo the video-caching arithmetic: truth 30 views with predictions 28 and 32 gives squared error 4 both ways but opposite cache decisions at the 30 boundary. Then state the classification alternative (no-cache, cheap-cache, expensive-cache labels) and when regression stays right (thresholds set and moving in app code).
traps: Calling the objective the metric. The objective is the single number the algorithm optimizes; metrics are everything reported. Rule 12 warns against confusing the directly optimized number with system health.
Treating a proxy as the goal. Liking, sharing, clicking, and watch time each mismeasure usefulness in a different direction; the table assigns one failure mode per proxy.
Writing causal conclusions from predictive wins. A higher click score does not show the ranking causes satisfaction; the clickbait paragraph shows behavior diverging after the intervention.

selfTest.q: Truth is 30 views; model A predicts 28 and model B predicts 32. Which has lower squared error, and which caches correctly at a 30-view cutoff?
selfTest.a: Neither has lower error: both miss by 2, so both have squared error 4. B caches (32 clears 30) while A does not, so equal loss hides opposite decisions.

selfTest.q: The team wants useful recommendations but logs only clicks. Name the proxy and two failure modes from the table.
selfTest.a: Proxy: predict click or play. Failures: it maximizes clickbait, and popularity prediction is not personalized; like-prediction separately misses most users who never click like.

selfTest.q: What distinguishes the ML objective from a success metric, per Rules 2, 12, 13 and the weather example?
selfTest.a: The objective is the single directly optimized number, kept simple, observable, and attributable (for example clicked). Success is product behavior (feature opened 50 percent more); a strong objective score need not move it.

selfTest.q: Why is the claim that the model proves longer videos are more useful a causal overclaim?
selfTest.a: Watch-time prediction favors long videos by construction, per the proxy table. Usefulness needs an experiment or policy comparison; the prediction only associates length with watched time under current exposure.
